slides.text:
A pointer does not always have a target. Its zero value is `nil`: it points at nothing, and reading through it stops the program.

In this module you check for nil, return it for missing results, use it for optional values and guard longer chains.
Pseudo code, not Go. A pointer is either empty or holds an address, and you ask which before you read through it.

A pointer you declare without a target is `nil`. You compare it with `== nil` or `!= nil`.

Pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
declare p, no target
p == nil is true

p = address of n
p == nil is false

slides.text: Reading through a nil pointer is not an error you can ignore: the program panics and stops. So code that may get a nil pointer checks first.

slides.text:
A function that may find nothing returns a pointer: the value when found, and nil when not. The caller checks before using it.

Pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
function pick(id)
    if id matches
        return address of user
    return nil

slides.text: Pointers also sit inside structs. Every step along a path can be nil, so check each one before the next step.

slides.text:
A method with a pointer receiver can be called on a nil pointer. The method runs, and receives nil.

A nil pointer can also stand for a missing setting, so the code falls back to a default. Setting a pointer to nil clears only that pointer, never the variable it pointed at.

exercises.title: Comparing pointers
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick your answer.
exercises.code:
var a, b *int
x := 1
c := &x
fmt.Println(a == b, a == nil, c == nil)
exercises.explanation: Two nil pointers are equal, and a nil pointer equals nil. c holds the address of x, so it is not nil.
